To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the inverse texture effect in the Great Plains is caused by an optimal soil moisture regime in which the dominant grasses experience little or no water stress during the growing season.

(i) the inverse texture effect in the Great Plains is reproduced by our coupled statistical-dynamical soil-water balance model, and (ii) the model is able to capture the seasonal cycle of the soil-water balance at the monthly timescales.

(1) the coupled SDEM and Shuttleworth-Wallce canopy model is able to capture the seasonal cycle of soil moisture and LAI at two sites in the Great Plains, (2) the mean peak LAI appears to be determined by the need to avoid leaf abscission due to water stress while maintaining the maximum possible rate of transpiration, and (3) the model is able to simulate the inverse texture effect, whereby vegetation productivity is highest in sandier soils.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of ecohydrological processes in the context of climate and vegetation dynamics, with the goal of providing a framework for studying the feedbacks between vegetation, climate, and soil.

developing an ecohydrological model of the monthly water balance that is able to capture the seasonal soil-water dynamics, the vegetation response to those dynamics, and the feedback of the vegetation on the soil-water dynamics.
developing and testing new methods for predicting the spatial and temporal variability of the water balance at the land surface.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the new model, SDEM, is a useful tool for studying the ecohydrology of grassland ecosystems.
the SDEM provides the first statistical-dynamical monthly model of the soil-water balance that is able to capture the seasonal variability of the water balance and vegetation dynamics.
the SDEM is able to simulate soil moisture and vegetation dynamics at monthly timescale with reasonable accuracy and with a minimum number of parameters.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SDEM is a useful tool to understand the interactions of climate, soil texture and vegetation in dry climates.

the SDEM can be used to estimate monthly mean soil moisture and evapotranspration for grassland ecosystems, and that it provides a new tool to study the controls of soil and climate on vegetation dynamics.

The main takeaway from our work is that

a monthly statistical-dynamically model of the water budget, when coupled with a two-component canopy evaporation model, is able to capture the seasonal cycle of soil moisture and the vegetation water balance.
the SDEM can be used to estimate monthly mean soil moisture and evapotranspirative water loss for a given climate and vegetation type.

the SDEM can be used to simulate the seasonal dynamics of soil moisture, vegetation density and evaporation at the monthly timescales, and that the model can reproduce the inverse texture effect in the absence of any parameterization that explicitly accounts for the soil water holding capacity.
